steps.title: The CA inventory
steps.body: Certification Authorities lists every CA in this instance with its status and expiry. From here you create a new CA, bring in an existing one, or open one to inspect its certificate and settings.

steps.title: Create a root of trust
steps.body: Create New CA builds a CA from scratch with a key that Lamassu generates and keeps. If the key is already registered in Lamassu, use Create New CA (Existing Key) instead.
steps.note: This example creates a root that issues directly. For an operational hierarchy, see Hierarchy and rotation.

steps.title: New key pair
steps.body: Lamassu generates the key pair inside a cryptographic engine and the private key stays there. You only download the public certificate.
steps.note: Which algorithms you can choose depends on what the engine supports.

steps.title: Key algorithm
steps.body: Each engine defines the algorithms and sizes it supports, such as RSA or ECDSA. ECDSA gives shorter keys and signatures than RSA at a comparable security level.

steps.title: Curve: P-384
steps.body: P-384 (secp384r1) offers roughly a 192-bit security level, above P-256, which makes it a common choice for long-lived roots.
steps.note: Check that the devices and validators that will verify this CA support the curve.

steps.title: CA name = Common Name
steps.body: The CA name must be unique and becomes the Common Name (CN) of the certificate subject. Because a root is self-signed, the same value is also its issuer.
steps.note: Name the authority after its purpose, not after a person.

steps.title: Country (C)
steps.body: Optional. Use the two-letter ISO 3166-1 code, here ES. Fill it only if your policy requires it.
steps.note: The subject is part of the signed certificate: changing it later means issuing a new certificate.

steps.title: Organization (O)
steps.body: Optional. The organization or team that operates the CA. It appears in the subject and, for issued certificates, in the issuer field.

steps.title: CA validity
steps.body: Enter a duration such as 1y, 365d or 2w. A CA must outlive the certificates it issues, so plan its validity longer than theirs.
steps.note: 1y is only for this evaluation. Issuance does not clamp a certificate to its issuer's expiry, so leave time to replace the CA.

steps.title: Issuance profile
steps.body: The profile is the default policy for certificates this CA issues: validity, subject handling and usages such as ClientAuth. Client Certificates suits device and user identities.
steps.note: Available profiles and their lifetimes depend on your environment.

steps.title: Create the authority
steps.body: Lamassu generates the key in the engine and signs the self-signed root certificate. The values you entered are fixed in that certificate once it is signed.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.body: Open the new CA and confirm its status is Active, plus its issuer, dates, engine and key.

steps.title: Certificate PEM
steps.body: The Certificate PEM tab holds the public CA certificate: download it as ca.pem. The private key never leaves the engine.
steps.note: Verify it with OpenSSL: CA:TRUE and a key usage that allows certificate signing. A valid self-signature does not install trust in other systems; distribute the root explicitly.
